mental_image: The curve became straight because I got close enough.

beats.title: Don't take my word for anything here
beats.body: This room has one idea in it, and you are going to *find* it — by moving things, guessing what happens next, and being wrong once or twice — before I give it a name. Nothing below is to be memorised. Predict, drag, and notice.
What is the *direction* of a curve at a single point?
beats.aside: A straight line has one obvious slope. A curve bends — steeper here than there. So what could "steepness" mean at a single point, where there is no second point to measure against? Hold the question. Don't answer it yet.

beats.body: Two points sit on this curve, joined by a straight line whose slope is easy — rise over run. **Drag the moving point toward the fixed one** and watch the slope number as the gap closes.

predict.body: Stop for a second — don't drag all the way yet. **Predict first:** as the gap keeps shrinking toward nothing, what does the slope do?

beats.reveal: Now finish the drag and see. It **settles** — the swinging stops and the slope closes in on one number instead of running away. Whatever you predicted, you have now *seen* what happens.

beats.body: But look at what that would need. A slope wants *two* points and the run between them. At the very end you want them to be the *same* point — run zero, rise zero, $0/0$, which means nothing.
beats.aside: So the honest slope needs two points, yet a direction-at-a-point wants one. That contradiction is the whole difficulty. Everything else in this room is how mathematics slips between its horns.

beats.body: Set the run aside and just *look* at the curve near the point. Drag the slider and zoom in. Keep going.
beats.reveal: There it is, and it is worth remembering above everything else in this room: **the curve became straight because you got close enough.** A smooth curve, seen closely enough, *is* a straight line — and a straight line has one definite slope.

beats.body: Do exactly what just worked. Put the fixed point on the sharp corner, drag the other point in, and **make the slope settle** the way it did before.
beats.reveal: It won't. Come in from the left and the slope says one thing; from the right, another. Nothing settles. Here mathematics simply *refuses* — at a corner there is no single direction, and no honest method can invent one. You didn't read that in a theorem; you just failed to do it.

beats.body: Put the three experiences together. The average slope over a shrinking step *settled*. Up close the curve *became* the straight line with that slope. And it exists only where the curve is smooth.
beats.after: That settled number is the answer to the question you were holding. It has a name — two, in fact. The number the average slopes *approach* is a **limit**. This particular limit is the **derivative**.

beats.kicker: Before I show you the formula — invent it
beats.body: You have felt the whole thing: a step $h$, an average slope, a number it approaches. **In symbols, how would you write the rule for that number?** Try — a rough attempt is worth more than a clean one you read.
beats.after: Whatever you wrote, hold it next to what comes now.

beats.body: Three and a half centuries ago, Newton and Leibniz were stuck on the very thing you just did by hand. This is what they wrote — read it as the sentence you already know:
beats.label: the derivative
beats.caption: Shrink the step $h$, watch the average slope, take the number it approaches. Not a formula handed to you — the answer to a problem you experienced.

beats.body: Take $f(x) = x^2$ and follow the definition — no rules, just the limit you now understand.
steps: Expand the numerator: (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2) / h
Let h approach 0: the leftover h vanishes
beats.label: for f(x) = x²
beats.after: Every rule you will meet — power, product, quotient, chain — is this same limit, worked out once so you never expand $(x+h)^n$ by hand again.

beats.body: This is position against time. Drag the moment $t$ and read the tangent's slope. That slope is the *speed at that instant* — the speedometer reading that felt impossible at the start.
beats.aside: Differentiate position and you get velocity. The abstract slope and the everyday speedometer are one object, seen twice.

beats.body: Here is a hill. Drag the point until the tangent lies perfectly flat. Where does that happen?
beats.aside: Exactly at the top. A maximum or minimum sits where the slope is zero — which is why every optimization problem becomes the single equation $f'(x) = 0$.

beats.kicker: Somewhere with no x in sight
beats.body: Forget calculus for a moment. This is a **seedling's height across two weeks**. Using only what you built today — no numbers given — drag to the day it was **growing fastest**. Judge by the tilt of the little line alone.
beats.reveal: That's the day. You just read the fastest change on a curve that has nothing to do with $x^2$ — a plant, not a parabola. That is the difference between learning a *procedure* and owning an *idea*: the idea travels.

beats.kicker: Before you leave — think, don't scroll
beats.body: You remember what you rebuild. Three rungs, hardest last; all kept only for you, to read again before the exam.

levels.prompt: Explain what a derivative is to a friend who has never taken calculus — two sentences, your words.
Sketch what happened when you zoomed in.
levels.draw: On paper: a curve, a point, and the tangent there — then the same point zoomed in until the curve *is* the line. Ten seconds; the drawing is the point, not its neatness.

levels.prompt: Imagine the derivative did *not* exist at some point. What would have to be true of the curve there? (You've already met one answer.)

beats.body: You arrived with a question and answered it with your own hands. Out of everything here — the formula, the names, Newton — the one thing worth keeping is not a symbol. It is a picture:
beats.image: The curve became straight because I got close enough.
beats.after: When an exam asks for a rate, a slope, a maximum, a velocity — close your eyes and zoom in. You are always being asked about this.
